content: The purpose of this clinical trial was to evaluate the safety and efficacy of long-term treatment with rosuvastatin, a statin medication, compared to a placebo. The study aimed to determine whether rosuvastatin could reduce the risk of major cardiovascular events, such as myocardial infarction, stroke, arterial revascularization, hospitalization for unstable angina, or death from cardiovascular causes. Additionally, the trial sought to assess the safety of rosuvastatin by monitoring total mortality, non-cardiovascular mortality, and adverse events, as well as its potential effects on the incidence of diabetes mellitus, venous thromboembolic events, and bone fractures. The study was a Phase III, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with a parallel assignment design. It enrolled 17,802 participants who were men aged 50 years or older and women aged 60 years or older. Eligible participants had low to normal levels of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol (<130 mg/dL) and elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) levels (>2.0 mg/L). Individuals with a history of cardiovascular or cerebrovascular events, active liver disease, diabetes mellitus, uncontrolled hypertension or hypothyroidism, certain malignancies, chronic inflammatory conditions, or a history of alcohol or drug abuse were excluded from the study. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either 20 mg of rosuvastatin daily or a placebo. The primary endpoint was the occurrence of major cardiovascular events, while secondary endpoints included safety outcomes and the incidence of other conditions such as diabetes and venous thromboembolism. The trial began in February 2003 and was initially planned to continue until August 2008. However, it was stopped early in March 2008 based on a recommendation from an Independent Data Monitoring Board and the JUPITER Steering Committee due to clear evidence of benefit in the rosuvastatin group. After a median follow-up period of 1.9 years (maximum of 5 years), the results demonstrated that rosuvastatin significantly reduced LDL cholesterol levels by 50% and hs-CRP levels by 37%. The rates of the primary endpoint were 0.77 and 1.36 per 100 person-years in the rosuvastatin and placebo groups, respectively, corresponding to a hazard ratio of 0.56 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.46 to 0.69; P<0.00001). Rosuvastatin also significantly reduced the rates of myocardial infarction (hazard ratio, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.30 to 0.70; P=0.0002), stroke (hazard ratio, 0.52; 95% CI, 0.34 to 0.79; P=0.002), and revascularization or unstable angina (hazard ratio, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.40 to 0.70; P<0.00001). The combined endpoint of myocardial infarction, stroke, or death from cardiovascular causes was also significantly reduced (hazard ratio, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.40 to 0.69; P<0.00001). Additionally, the rate of death from any cause was lower in the rosuvastatin group (hazard ratio, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.67 to 0.97; P=0.02). The effects of rosuvastatin were consistent across all subgroups evaluated. Importantly, there was no significant increase in the incidence of myopathy or cancer in the rosuvastatin group. However, there was a higher incidence of physician-reported diabetes in participants receiving rosuvastatin. In conclusion, this trial demonstrated that in apparently healthy individuals without hyperlipidemia but with elevated hs-CRP levels, rosuvastatin significantly reduced the incidence of major cardiovascular events. These findings highlight the potential benefit of rosuvastatin in reducing cardiovascular risk in a population with elevated inflammatory markers, even in the absence of elevated LDL cholesterol levels.
